title: De transformatione serierum in fractiones continuas, ubi simul haec theoria non mediocriter amplificatur

deep.reconstruction:
This page is the end of §49 and the start of Problem V (§50).

(1) Conclusion of §49. From Theorem VIII with α=1, β=2, γ=3, …, the series s = x/y − x²/(2y²) + x³/(6y³) − … equals 1 − e^{−x/y}. This gives
x/(1−e^{−x/y}) = x e^{x/y}/(e^{x/y}−1) = y + xy/(2y−x + 2xy/(3y−x + 3xy/(4y−x + …))).
Setting x=1 and y=n (n=1,2,3,4) gives special cases:
- e/(e−1) = 1 + 1/(1 + 2/(2 + 3/(3 + …)));
- √e/(√e−1) = 2 + 2/(3 + 4/(5 + 6/(7 + …)));
- e^{1/3}/(e^{1/3}−1) = 3 + 3/(5 + 6/(8 + 9/(11 + …)));
- e^{1/4}/(e^{1/4}−1) = 4 + 4/(7 + 8/(11 + 12/(15 + …))).
In general, e^{1/n}/(e^{1/n}−1) = n + n/((2n−1) + 2n/((3n−1) + 3n/((4n−1) + …))).

(2) Problem V, §50. Take the general alternating series s = Σ_{k≥1} (−1)^{k−1} (a b c ⋯)(x/y)^k/(α β γ ⋯), whose ratio of successive terms is −(next Latin letter)·x/((next Greek letter)·y). Define the tails t (starting from b/β) and u (starting from c/γ). Then:
- s = (ax/(αy))(1−t);
- ax/s = αy/(1−t) = αy + αyt/(1−t) = αy + αbxy/(−bx + bx/t);
- likewise bx/t = βy + βcxy/(−cx + cx/u), and so on.
Repeated substitution gives
ax/s = αy + αbxy/(βy − bx + βcxy/(γy − cx + γdxy/(δy − dx + …))).
The next page states this as Theorem IX and applies it to the incomplete beta-type integral ∫z^{m−1}(1+z^n)^{k/n−1}dz.

This is Euler's standard conversion of a series into an equivalent continued fraction: its n-th approximant equals the n-th partial sum. Here it is written in a two-parameter-per-step hypergeometric-ratio form.
errors: None in substance. I verified the special cases numerically: for y=1 the tail 1 + 2/(2 + 3/(3 + …)) evaluates to 1.7183… = e−1, so 1 + 1/(e−1) = e/(e−1). The cases y=2, 3, 4 follow correctly from the general formula with partial denominators (k+1)n−1 and numerators kn.

Minor: the solution of Problem V assumes nonvanishing tails (t≠0, 1−t≠0). As usual, Euler gives no convergence discussion. Because the continued fraction is equivalent to the series, there is no acceleration; it converges exactly when the series does.

ideas.what: Continued fraction for x/(1−e^{−x/y}) and the special cases e^{1/n}/(e^{1/n}−1), including e/(e−1) = 1 + 1/(1 + 2/(2 + 3/(3 + …))), equivalently e−1 = 1 + 2/(2 + 3/(3 + …))
ideas.modern_name: Euler-type continued fraction for the exponential; Euler's continued fraction e = 2 + 1/(1 + 1/(2 + 2/(3 + …)))
ideas.where_published: Closely related expansions of e appear in Euler's E71 (De fractionibus continuis dissertatio, 1737/44) and the Introductio (E101, 1748, ch. 18). The particular n-th-root family here is in this paper, E593.

ideas.what: Conversion of a series with term ratio −(b x)/(β y) etc. into an equivalent continued fraction whose approximants are the partial sums
ideas.modern_name: Euler's continued fraction formula (series ↔ equivalent continued fraction)
ideas.where_published: Introductio in analysin infinitorum I, ch. 18 (E101); generalized here in E593 (Theorem IX)

deep.surprise_reason: Both results are applications of Euler's well-known series-to-continued-fraction transformation, and the e-expansions are classical and credited to Euler. The family of expansions for e^{1/n}/(e^{1/n}−1) is a trivial specialization. The function x/(1−e^{−x}) is the Bernoulli-number generating function, but Euler draws no such link and the continued fraction (being merely equivalent to the series) yields nothing new about it.
transcription_corrections: In §50 the phrase 'ex relatione bx/(βy)(1−u)' should read 'ex relatione t = bx/(βy)(1−u)'. The 't =' is missing in the transcription; the scan reads roughly 'ex relatione (bx/βy)(1−u) fiet'.
The top line of p.168 continues §49: '= x e^{x/y}/(e^{x/y}−1)'. This is correctly transcribed.
